title: Whether glory is due inherent justice: deferred; promise by fittingness
source_text: XXXVII. An autem justitiae quae per Spiritus Sancti gratiam fidelibus inest gloria debeatur, ut contendit Bellarminus, alia quaestio est, quam, Deo favente, alias expendemus, quum de bonorum operum meritis ex professo agemus. Id solum breviter dicimus, quantumlibet bonis hominum operibus per se nihil a Deo deberi: attamen Deum justitiae, & sanctitati fidelium, coronam vitae & gloriae coelestis liberaliter promisisse, & juxta promissa sua misericorditer simul & fideliter esse redditurum, quum olim mortuos & vivos judicabit. Qua in re non exercebit proprie dictam illam justitiam, qua aliquis exsolvit quod stricto jure debet, sed tantum justitiam communi quadam ratione sic dictam, quae est, ut vetustiores Scholastici loquuntur, condecentia bonitatis divinae, & ad quam pertinet fides in promissis servandis. Quod major & sanior pars Scholae Pontificiae nobiscum ultro fatetur & agnoscit.
pass_a_gloss: But whether glory is due to the righteousness that is in the faithful by the Holy Spirit’s grace, as Bellarmine contends, is another question which, God favoring, we shall weigh elsewhere when we treat expressly of the merits of good works. This only we say briefly: however much nothing is owed by God to men’s good works of themselves, yet God has liberally promised to the faithful’s righteousness and holiness the crown of life and heavenly glory, and according to his promises will mercifully and faithfully render it when he one day judges the dead and the living. In which matter he will not exercise that justice properly so called by which someone pays what he owes by strict right, but only justice so called in a certain common sense, which is, as the older Scholastics speak, the fittingness of divine goodness, and to which belongs faithfulness in keeping promises. Which the greater and sounder part of the Pontifical school freely confesses and acknowledges with us.
pass_b_english: Whether glory is strictly due inherent justice is deferred to merits; works per se are owed nothing.
God promised the crown and will keep it by fitting goodness and promise-faithfulness—as saner Rome grants.
